title: Cubism: Picasso and Braque
subject: art
description: Between 1907 and 1920, **Picasso** and **Braque** broke the object into facets seen from several angles at once. The most radical revolution since the Renaissance.

hero.hook: What if a painting were no longer a window, but an object rebuilt from every angle?

blocks.text: Cubism was born between **1907** and **1908**. It may be the most radical revolution since the perspective of the [[Quattrocento]], the Italian 15th century. **Pablo Picasso** and **Georges Braque** broke the object into geometric fragments.
The painting as a window onto the world was finished. The painter no longer copied nature; he rebuilt it. That deconstruction opened the way to abstract art.

sections.title: Cézanne and the shock of the masks

blocks.text: Before Cubism, **Paul Cézanne** looked for the solid form behind the shifting light. His advice was to “treat nature by means of the cylinder, the sphere, the cone.” In his views of Mont Sainte-Victoire, he flattened space and multiplied viewpoints with [[passages]], those zones where planes melt into each other.

blocks.caption: Cézanne: nature seen as an assembly of volumes

blocks.text: In 1907, Picasso described his visit to the Trocadéro museum not as a lesson in beauty but as an exorcism in the face of the masks' power.

In **1907**, at the ethnography museum at the [[Trocadéro]], Picasso discovered [[African and Oceanic arts]]. The masks do not copy a face; they turn it into a concept. The object was no longer painted as it is seen, but as it is known.
In **1907**, Picasso finished *Les Demoiselles d'Avignon*. Five nudes cut into sharp facets, and some of the faces become masks. Even [[Apollinaire]], his poet friend, was stunned.

blocks.caption: Les Demoiselles d'Avignon: the point of no return

blocks.text: From **1908** to **1912**, Picasso and Braque invented **analytic Cubism**. They studied a volume from every angle, then laid all those views on the canvas at once. Color almost vanished: grays and ochres, to force the eye onto space. Small clues, a key or a guitar string, keep the picture from tipping into pure abstraction.
They took the collaboration so far that they sometimes dressed as workmen, to stress the craft side of what they were doing.

Around **1912**, with the risk that nobody could read the paintings anymore, they invented **synthetic Cubism**. The object was no longer chopped into a thousand fragments; it was summed up by its clearest signs. This is where [[collage]] appears: newspaper and wallpaper pasted onto the canvas.
Braque, a former house painter, used a steel comb to fake wood grain so well that it looked truer than the real wood pasted beside it.
Color came back. Forms grew wider. A guitar could be nothing but a curve. The painting was no longer a mirror: it was an object in its own right, built by its own laws.

sections.title: A legacy that spills past painting

blocks.text: Cubism spread fast. **Juan Gris** brought it a mathematical rigor. The [[Puteaux Group]] bent it toward the aesthetic of the machine. The movement fed Italian Futurism and Mondrian's abstraction, and it shaped [[graphic design]] as much as architecture.

events.title: Collage and synthetic Cubism
events.detail: Reality entered the work in fragments.

blocks.text: Above all, the viewer became active: the image has to be put back together by whoever is looking. Art finally broke away from simple imitation.
By breaking Renaissance perspective and inventing collage, Picasso and Braque turned the painting into mental architecture rather than a mirror of the world.
